First, I need to recall which problems are still open in 2025. Poincaré is already solved, so the remaining six are the targets. Solving any of these is a huge deal, and all require groundbreaking work.

Now, considering AI's role. As of 2023, AI like me is good at pattern recognition and assisting in proofs, but creating entirely new mathematical arguments hasn't been done yet. However, by 2026, maybe more advanced systems will be around. I should think about how likely AI integration into solving these problems becomes. 

For early dates like 2026, the chance might be low. Maybe a 0.1 or so. As time goes on, with AI advancements, the probability could increase. By 2050, it's plausible that AI has matured to the point of contributing novel proofs. But how much?

Also, the problems vary in nature. P vs NP is more computational, maybe amenable to AI techniques. Navier-Stokes is analytical. The Hodge conjecture is algebraic geometry, more abstract. So some might be more accessible to AI approaches than others.

I need to balance the time for AI to develop with the inherent difficulty of the problems. Even with AI, these are hard. The event requires not just AI contribution but a complete solution that meets Clay's standards.

So maybe assign probabilities that go from 10% in 2026, increasing each decade. Let me think. By 2030, 15%, 2035 25%, 2040 40%, 2050 perhaps 60%? But I need to ensure the probabilities are non-decreasing and account for the event possibly never happening. Also, even 60% by 2050 might be too low, but given the uncertainty, maybe that's the best estimate.
</think>

formatted_prompt:
<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2025-04-29. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
